query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting as-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA to a two-step cryogenic-then-warm rolling process, followed by a short anneal at around 700 °C, will refine the lamellar microstructure, increase heterogeneous interfaces, and enhance both yield strength and ductility simultaneously.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy containing FCC/B2 lamellae
generation.intervention: After casting, apply heavy cold deformation at cryogenic temperatures, then moderate warm rolling, followed by short-time annealing at about 700 °C
generation.conditions: Maintain cryo-rolling at −196 °C, then warm roll at ~400 °C, followed by brief annealing (~15–30 minutes) at 700 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement of lamella spacing and formation of heterogeneous interfaces (partially recrystallized, ultrafine features) during annealing
generation.mechanism: The refined lamellar structure and increased density of heterogeneous interfaces promote enhanced strain hardening and crack-arrest capability, leading to improved strength–ductility synergy
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, yield strength increases by at least 30% while ductility remains equal or moderately higher
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 without post-casting thermomechanical treatment
generation.boundary: Effective improvement requires adequate cryo-rolling strains, warm-rolling temperatures below full recrystallization thresholds, and a short anneal that avoids excessive grain growth
generation.uncertainty: Exact gains depend on rolling reductions and hold times; insufficient rolling or overly long annealing may reduce the synergistic effect and degrade ductility

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sample sets: (1) as-cast (baseline), (2) cryo-rolled only, (3) cryo-rolled + warm-rolled + 700 °C anneal. Compare microstructures via SEM/TEM and assess tensile strength and elongation at room temperature. Test if the third set outperforms the baseline in both strength and ductility.
measurements: Grain size, phase fraction and interface density via SEM/TEM
Tensile yield strength and total elongation at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combination of increased yield strength and equal or improved ductility is not observed in the cryo-rolled + warm-rolled + annealed samples relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The present study for the first time demonstrated that cryo-deformation and annealing could be a novel microstructural design strategy for overcoming strength-ductility trade off in multiphase high ent

It is rather interesting to note that certain intermetallic phases such as Fe3Al also show simultaneous increase in strength and ductility in recovered or partially recrystallized conditions (having a few recrystallized grains),. While the mechanisms responsible for this rather interesting behavior of Fe3Al have not been investigated in-depth, the simultaneous increase in strength and ductility of the cryo-rolled and annealed material with hierarchical microstructure composed of ultrafine recrystallized, recovered and partially recrystallized phases is evidently in excellent agreement,. In summary, the effect of thermo-mechanical processing by cryo-rolling and annealing on microstructure and properties of nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA was investigated. The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure after annealing. The synergistic effect exerted by the hierarchical microstructure resulted in outstanding increase in strength without loss of ductility when compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases to jointly boost ductility and strength. Subsequent studies (PMC5818523, PMC6353877) refined this idea through cryo-rolling and carefully controlled annealing to produce hierarchically ultrafine lamellae and duplex/multiscale structures. More recent efforts (PMC6687781) combined cryogenic and warm deformation to induce compositional and structural heterogeneities, further enhancing strength–ductility synergy. Over time, processing routes that create hierarchically refined lamellae and phase-scale heterogeneities have repeatedly improved performance, yet there remain open questions about how to consistently scale these approaches while retaining or maximizing both strength and ductility.
decision.unsolved: The main challenge is developing robust, easily scalable processing routes to refine the lamellar structure, preserve phase balance, and control the heterogeneities in eutectic high-entropy alloys without sacrificing either strength or ductility. Industrial-scale demonstrations and systematic validation of these processes under real-world service conditions remain incomplete.
decision.lever: Implement a two-step cryo-then-warm rolling protocol on an as-cast eutectic HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) followed by short-time annealing at ~700 °C to refine the lamellae, increase the density of heterogeneous interfaces, and achieve balanced strengthening and toughening.
decision.why: Prior investigations of EHEAs have shown that enhanced strength and ductility can be achieved by introducing and stabilizing ultrafine lamellar structures through cryogenic and mild warm deformations combined with partial recrystallization. This approach is directly supported by recent studies demonstrating that refined lamella spacing and heterogeneous interfaces promote strain hardening and arrest microcrack propagation, thus providing the sought-after synergy of higher strength and ductility. The proposed protocol is a logical extension of these trends, geared toward manufacturing readiness and performance optimization.
